lesson.title: Interest Rates and Central Banks
lesson.summary: How central banks use interest rates to control the economy and what that means for you.

blocks.text: An interest rate is the cost of money over time. When you borrow, you pay interest. When you save, you earn interest. Central banks control the economy's base rate.
The role of the central bank

In the US, the Federal Reserve controls the Fed Funds rate. In the EU, the European Central Bank sets its key rates. These base rates influence the entire financial system: credit, savings, and exchange rates.

items: High rates: credit becomes expensive, consumption falls, inflation retreats
Low rates: credit becomes cheap, consumption rises, economy accelerates
The challenge: calibrating without causing recession or runaway inflation

blocks.text: The central bank has only one instrument, which is the short-term interest rate. — Ben Bernanke

cards.front: What is the Federal Reserve's main policy tool?
cards.back: The federal funds rate — the interest rate at which banks lend to each other overnight. It influences all other rates in the financial system.

cards.front: Why does a central bank raise interest rates?
cards.back: To reduce inflation: higher rates make credit more expensive, reduce consumption, and decrease demand for goods and services.

cards.front: What is the risk of cutting rates too much?
cards.back: It can generate excessive inflation by stimulating demand beyond the economy's productive capacity.

quiz.question: When a central bank wants to reduce inflation, it typically:
options: Lowers interest rates to stimulate growth
Raises interest rates to make credit more expensive
Prints more money to cover expenses
quiz.explanation: Higher rates make credit more expensive, reduce consumption and demand, which tends to curb inflation.

quiz.question: What can happen when interest rates stay too low for too long?
options: Asset bubbles and excessive inflation can develop
quiz.explanation: Very low rates encourage excessive credit and speculation, which can create market bubbles and inflationary pressure.
